---
title: "The Working Draft"
---

::: {.landing}
:::

This book collects two teaching notes that were written separately but belong together.

The first, on scientific writing, grew out of workshops I have been running for doctoral students at the Faculty of Medicine of the University of Porto since the early 2010s. The second, on data visualisation, started as a companion piece — the images that sit between the words. Both notes were published individually on [tiagojct.eu](https://tiagojct.eu), and both were used in teaching before any thought was given to combining them.

The case for combining them is straightforward. A figure is part of a paper. A paper is more than its figures. The two sets of decisions — what to write and how to show it — are made by the same person, for the same readers, under the same editorial pressure. Teaching them together respects that reality.

The book is written for three overlapping readers: doctoral students in clinical research, doctoral students in health data science, and medical undergraduates taking their first steps into research. What they share is the task of turning work into a paper others can read, check, and build on. Prior statistical exposure helps but is not assumed everywhere; terms are defined on first use and collected in the [glossary](chapters/glossary.qmd). The approach is practical rather than theoretical. Every principle is followed immediately by an example, and the examples run through the same datasets across the book so that the visual choices, the writing choices, and the analysis can be read against each other.

Part I covers the architecture and craft of scientific writing: the structure of a journal article, the mechanics of clear prose, the presentation of data in text and tables, the editorial process, reporting guidelines, reference management, co-authorship, and workflow. Part II covers the decisions that produce a figure worth looking at: the encoding choices, the common chart types, the failure modes, captions, colour, and the responsible use of AI for figure construction. Part III covers the analysis beneath the paper — reporting a clinical prediction model to the standard such models are held to, and making the code and data reproducible enough that another researcher can rerun them.

The parts share a palette, a typeface, and a fictional heart-failure cohort in Part I (reused in Part III) and a hypertension cohort in Part II — all simulated for the examples alone. They also share the underlying conviction that good research communication is a learnable set of habits, not a talent you either have or you don't.

**How to read it.** If you are actively writing a paper, read Part I in order. If you have data but have not yet started writing, begin with Chapters 1, 3, and 9. If you are new to research — a medical undergraduate, or at the stage where research still happens to other people — start with Chapters 1 and 3, keep the [glossary](chapters/glossary.qmd) open, and return to the structural and compliance chapters when you have a study in front of you. If you work in data and code, Part III (prediction models, reproducibility) is written for you and can be read after Chapter 4 and the statistical-writing chapter. Part II can be read independently at any stage. The [quick reference](chapters/guide.qmd) and the [checklists](chapters/checklists.qmd) are there for when you need a specific answer fast.

Tiago Jacinto\
Porto, May 2026
